claims.text: Al and Cr exhibit inherently sluggish diffusion in Al-Cr-Fe-Ni-Co-based high-entropy alloys.
Sluggish diffusion restricts the outward transport of Al and Cr during high-temperature exposure.
Restricted outward transport of Al and Cr leads to formation of a mixed Al2O3/Cr2O3 oxide layer.
The resulting mixed Al2O3/Cr2O3 layer is self-limiting, uniform, adherent, and protective.
The initial alloy is a single-phase Al-Cr-Fe-Ni-Co-based high-entropy alloy.
The initial alloy has a homogeneous elemental distribution.
Al and Cr concentrations will be varied systematically while the other alloying elements are maintained constant.
Oxidation tests will expose samples to air at 900–1100 °C for 100 hours under controlled oxygen partial pressures.
Differential diffusion kinetics of reactive elements govern oxide-layer growth.
Sluggish diffusion in the HEA matrix limits the supply of Al and Cr to the oxide/metal interface.
Limited Al and Cr cation flux promotes nucleation and retention of the mixed Al2O3/Cr2O3 layer.
The mixed oxide layer remains thin and adherent and inhibits further oxidation.
Relative to a conventional faster-diffusing alloy, the HEA will form a thinner oxide layer.
Relative to a conventional faster-diffusing alloy, the HEA will form a more uniform oxide layer.
Relative to a conventional faster-diffusing alloy, the HEA will show lower oxygen penetration.
The baseline conventional binary or simpler alloys have higher elemental diffusion rates.
Under the same oxidation conditions, the baseline alloys form thicker, less uniform, and less adherent oxide layers.
The proposed mechanism applies at 900–1100 °C in single-phase, compositionally controlled HEAs.
Significant microstructural heterogeneity or phase transformations may invalidate the proposed mechanism.

A lack of correlation between Al/Cr concentration, measured diffusion behavior, and oxide-scale characteristics—together with oxide layers comparable to the fast-diffusing baseline—would falsify the hypothesis.
